choices.rationale: lstatSync deliberately does not follow the link, so it reports the link entry and isSymbolicLink() is true.
statSync resolves the link and reports the target's real size, not a placeholder of 0.
That would be the length of the stored target path, which is what lstat reports; statSync reports the target file's size.

query.explanation: `lstatSync` describes the link itself, so `isSymbolicLink()` is true. `statSync` follows the link and describes the target, so its `size` is the target's 11-byte payload (`hello world`). Only `lstat` would report the link's own size, which is the byte length of the stored target path.

choices.rationale: A name that starts with a dot and has no other dot is treated as having no extension, so '.bashrc' returns '' rather than itself.
'index.' ends in a dot, and extname returns that trailing '.' instead of an empty string.
extname looks only at the last segment, so the dot in the directory part of 'a.b/c' is ignored.

query.title: path.extname edge cases

choices.rationale: Only one '..' would climb from '/a/b/c' to '/a/b', which is not the common ancestor '/a' of the two paths.
relative returns a relative path, not the target itself; it returns an absolute path only when no relative route exists.
Three '..' segments would climb past '/a' to the filesystem root, overshooting the shared prefix by one level.

questions.code:
const path = require('node:path');

console.log(path.posix.relative('/a/b/c', '/a/d'));

query.explanation: relative(from, to) finds the longest common prefix ('/a'), emits one '..' for each remaining segment of from ('b' and 'c'), then appends the remaining segments of to ('d'), giving '../../d'.
query.title: path.relative walks up to the common root

choices.rationale: A reference that supplies a path replaces the base query, so the base's '?q=1' is not inherited.
That treats the base as '/a/b/c/' with two levels removed; the last base segment 'c' is a file, so only 'b' is popped.
That is the result for plain 'g'; the leading '..' removes one more directory level before appending 'g'.

questions.code: console.log(new URL('../g', 'https://ex.com/a/b/c?q=1#h').href);

query.explanation: The base path '/a/b/c' contributes its directory '/a/b/', then '..' pops 'b' and 'g' is appended, giving '/a/g'. A relative reference with its own path discards the base's query and fragment, so '?q=1' and '#h' are dropped.

choices.rationale: A port matching the scheme default is discarded during parsing, so ':443' never appears in an https href.
Only the scheme and host are case-normalized; path, query, and fragment keep the case they were written with.
Dot segments are resolved while parsing a hierarchical URL, so '/Path/..' collapses away instead of being kept.

questions.code:
const u = new URL('HTTPS://Example.COM:443/Path/../Other?A=B#Frag');

console.log(u.href);

query.explanation: The parser lowercases the scheme and host, omits a port equal to the scheme's default (443 for https), and removes dot segments from the path. Path, query, and fragment text keep their original case, so '/Other?A=B#Frag' is preserved verbatim.

choices.rationale: The form-urlencoded serializer writes a space as '+'; %20 is what the URL path serializer uses instead.
A literal '+' in the value must be escaped as %2B, otherwise it would decode back as a space.
toString always escapes the value, since an unescaped space and '&' would change the parsed parameter list.

query.explanation: toString uses the application/x-www-form-urlencoded serializer: a space becomes '+', and characters that are structurally meaningful are percent-encoded, so '+' becomes %2B and '&' becomes %26.
query.title: URLSearchParams serialization

choices.rationale: Leaving '#' literal would make '1.txt' a fragment rather than part of the file name, so it is escaped as %23.
A space is not a legal URL character and is serialized as %20, and '#' is escaped so the name survives round-tripping.
With two slashes 'tmp' would be parsed as the host; pathToFileURL emits an empty host, giving 'file:///'.

questions.code:
const { pathToFileURL } = require('node:url');

console.log(pathToFileURL('/tmp/my file#1.txt').href);

query.explanation: pathToFileURL escapes characters that would otherwise change the URL's structure, so '#' becomes %23 instead of starting a fragment, and the URL serializer encodes the space as %20. The host is empty, which is why the href has three slashes.
query.title: pathToFileURL escaping

questions.code:
const path = require('node:path');

console.log(path.win32.isAbsolute('C:/foo'), path.posix.isAbsolute('C:/foo'));

query.explanation: The win32 implementation treats a drive letter followed by a separator as absolute, while the posix implementation only considers a leading '/' absolute, so 'C:/foo' is a relative posix path.
query.title: isAbsolute differs per platform flavor

questions.rationale: The posix flavor has no notion of drive letters, so 'C:/foo' is relative there even though win32 reports it as absolute.

questions.code:

console.log(path.posix.join('/foo', 'bar', '/baz'));

query.title: join does not restart at an absolute segment

questions.rationale: Restarting at a later absolute segment is resolve's behavior; join just glues the segments together, so the output is '/foo/bar/baz'.

query.explanation: For a basename whose only dot is the leading one, parse reports the whole basename as name and an empty ext, so the array is ['.gitignore', ''].

questions.rationale: A leading dot does not begin an extension, so name is '.gitignore' and ext is '', giving ['.gitignore', ''] instead.

query.explanation: delete removes every entry with the given name, not just the first, and the URL's search is re-serialized after each mutation. The appended value's space is serialized as '+' by the form-urlencoded serializer.

questions.rationale: delete('a') drops both 'a' entries and the searchParams object writes back through to url.search, where the appended space becomes '+'.

choices.rationale: Assumes reassigning `exports` also replaces `module.exports`; it only rebinds the local parameter, so neither property reaches the loaded value.
Assumes `exports.b = 2` lands on the original exports object, but after the reassignment `exports` points at the new `{ a: 1 }` object.
Assumes the last whole-object assignment to `exports` becomes the module's value; only `module.exports` has that power.

query.explanation: `exports` is just a parameter of the module wrapper that initially points at the same object as `module.exports`. Assigning `exports = { a: 1 }` rebinds only that local name, so `exports.b = 2` mutates the detached object. `require` returns `module.exports`, which is still the untouched empty object, so `{}` is printed.
query.syntax: module.exports = value; // replaces exports; `exports = value` does not
query.title: exports rebinding vs module.exports

choices.rationale: Assumes the cycle re-enters `mod_a3.js` and finishes it first; `b` really sees only the partial exports of `a`, which lacks `bName`.
Reverses the situation: `a` finishes after `b` returns, so `a.bName` is set, while `b.aSawB` was snapshotted too early.
Assumes a cycle makes both requires yield empty exports; `a` still completes its assignment after `require` of `b` returns.

query.explanation: Loading `mod_a3.js` sets `name`, then requires `mod_b3.js`, which requires `mod_a3.js` back. Because `mod_a3.js` is already in the cache, `b` receives its *partial* exports `{ name: 'a' }`, so `a.bName` is still `undefined` when `aSawB` is captured. Control returns to `a`, which then sets `bName = 'b'`.
query.syntax: require(id) // returns module.exports as it exists right now
query.title: Circular require returns partial exports

choices.rationale: Assumes deleting the cache entry has no effect; removing it forces the file to be compiled and evaluated again, bumping the counter.
Assumes every `require` re-evaluates the file, but the second call is served from `require.cache` without running the body.
Assumes the counter also increments for cached lookups; the module body runs only twice in total, so the last value is 2.

query.explanation: The first `require` evaluates the file and the counter becomes 1. The second `require` is a cache hit and returns the same exported value without running the body. Deleting `require.cache[require.resolve(p)]` drops the cached Module, so the third `require` evaluates the file again and exports 2.
query.title: require.cache and re-evaluation

choices.rationale: Counts `exports`, `require`, `module` and `__filename` but leaves out `__dirname`, which is also injected into the wrapper.
Counts only `exports`, `require` and `module`; the two path variables are wrapper parameters too, not globals.
Assumes just `module` and `exports` are passed in, but `require`, `__filename` and `__dirname` are parameters as well.

query.explanation: Node wraps every CommonJS file in a function declared as `(exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname)`. Inside the module body, `arguments` therefore has length 5, which is why those five names look like globals but are actually locals.
query.title: The CommonJS module wrapper arity

choices.rationale: Assumes `b` holds the number 3; the JSON value is the string "3", so `+ 1` concatenates instead of adding.
Assumes requiring a `.json` file yields the raw file text; the JSON loader parses it, so `typeof` is `object`.
Assumes `+` coerces the string operand numerically and fails; with a string on the left, `+` performs concatenation and never yields NaN here.

query.explanation: The CommonJS `.json` loader reads the file and sets `module.exports = JSON.parse(text)`, so `d` is a plain object (`typeof` is `'object'`). `d.b` is the string `"3"`, and `"3" + 1` concatenates to `"31"`.
query.title: Requiring a JSON file

choices.rationale: Assumes the argument is treated as a directory; `createRequire` treats it as a filename, so relative ids resolve against its parent directory.
Assumes resolution fails because `/tmp/m9dir` is not a real file; the path only needs to be absolute, not existing.
Assumes `createRequire` validates that the path points at a file; it accepts any absolute path or file URL string.

query.explanation: `createRequire(filename)` builds a require whose base is `path.dirname(filename)`. Passing `/tmp/m9dir` means the base is `/tmp`, so `./dep9.js` loads `/tmp/dep9.js` and prints `outer`. To target the directory's contents you must pass something like `/tmp/m9dir/noop.js` or `/tmp/m9dir/`.
query.title: createRequire resolves relative to the filename's directory

choices.rationale: Assumes `index.js` always wins for a directory; it is only the fallback when `package.json` has no usable `main` field.
Assumes require hands back the `main` field's string; the loader uses that field as a path and returns the loaded module's exports.
Assumes directory specifiers are rejected in CommonJS; the loader resolves directories via `package.json` `main` or `index.js`.

query.explanation: When a CommonJS specifier resolves to a directory, Node reads `package.json` and, if `main` is present and loadable, resolves that path relative to the directory. Here `main` is `lib/entry.js`, so `/tmp/m10dir/lib/entry.js` is loaded and `index.js` is ignored.
query.title: Directory resolution via package.json main

choices.rationale: Removing the cache entry forces Node to load and run the file again, so the third require sees an incremented counter rather than the original value.
A cached require returns the stored exports without re-running the module body, so the second call cannot increment the counter.
Deleting the cache entry only drops the stored exports; the next require reloads the file from disk and returns its new exports value.

query.explanation: CommonJS modules run once per resolved filename: the first require executes the body (hits becomes 1) and stores the exports in require.cache, so the second require returns the same cached value 1 without running the file again. Deleting the cache entry keyed by require.resolve(file) makes the third require load and execute the file a second time, so global.hits increments to 2 and the fresh exports value is 2.
query.title: require.cache controls module re-execution

query.explanation: When a require specifier has no extension, Node tries the exact filename first, then appends extensions in the fixed order .js, .json, .node. Both widget.js and widget.json exist here, but .js is tried first, so the JavaScript module wins and its exports object has kind 'js'. Creation order on disk is irrelevant; only the fixed extension order matters.
query.syntax: require('./widget') // tries widget, widget.js, widget.json, widget.node
query.title: Extension resolution order for extensionless requires

questions.rationale: The .json file is never reached: Node appends .js before .json when resolving an extensionless path, so widget.js is loaded even though widget.json was written first.

query.explanation: If a module body throws while loading, Node deletes its entry from require.cache so the failure is not memoized. The first require sets global.seen and throws, so first is 'boom'. The second require reloads and re-executes the file; global.seen is now truthy, the throw is skipped, and module.exports becomes the string 'ok'. The program therefore prints 'boom ok'.
query.syntax: try { require(id) } catch (err) { /* module removed from cache */ }
query.title: A module that throws is not left in require.cache

questions.rationale: The failed load is removed from require.cache instead of being cached, so the second require runs the body again; global.seen is already set, so it exports 'ok' and the line is `boom ok`.

choices.rationale: errorMonitor listeners are invoked before the regular 'error' listeners, not after them.
errorMonitor only observes the event; it does not swallow it, so the 'error' listener still runs.
The errorMonitor listener is registered for this emitter and is called on every emitted 'error'.

query.explanation: `events.errorMonitor` installs an observer for 'error' events. Its listeners run before the regular 'error' listeners and do not consume the event, so the normal 'error' handler still runs afterwards. Because a real 'error' listener exists, nothing is thrown.
query.title: events.errorMonitor

query.explanation: When every input promise rejects, `Promise.any` rejects with an `AggregateError` whose `errors` array holds the individual reasons in input order, so the name is `AggregateError` and `errors.length` is 2.
query.title: Promise.any rejection shape

questions.rationale: Both inputs reject, so Promise.any rejects with an AggregateError carrying both reasons in `errors`, giving length 2.

choices.rationale: `cause` is defined directly on the error instance, not inherited from Error.prototype, so hasOwnProperty returns true.

The options object's `cause` is honoured by the Error constructor, so `e.cause` is set rather than undefined.

console.log(`${e.cause.name} ${Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(e, 'cause')}`);

choices.rationale: Node documents these as system errors but does not change `name`; it remains 'Error'.
`syscall` names the underlying OS call that failed, which is 'open', not the JavaScript API used.
TypeError is used for bad argument types; a missing path produces a generic Error with code ENOENT.

choices.rationale: The DOM-compatible code string used by Node for aborts is 'ABORT_ERR'; ERR_ABORTED is not the code on this error.
Node sets the error's `name` to 'AbortError' so callers can detect cancellation by name.
Node's timers/promises rejects with an AbortError instance whose name is 'AbortError', not with a DOMException named that way.

choices.rationale: An emitted Error instance is rethrown unchanged, so the first caught value keeps the name RangeError.
A non-Error payload is wrapped in a Node error that carries the code ERR_UNHANDLED_ERROR.
emit does not type-check its payload; the string simply becomes an unhandled 'error' reported as ERR_UNHANDLED_ERROR.

choices.rationale: On error Node invokes the callback with only the error argument, so `data` is undefined rather than null or a Buffer.
ENOTDIR appears when a path component exists but is not a directory; here the component does not exist at all, giving ENOENT.
The code is ENOENT for a missing path component, and the omitted result argument makes `data` undefined.

query.explanation: Node's callback convention passes the error first; on failure the remaining result arguments are simply omitted, so `data` is `undefined` (not `null` or an empty Buffer). A missing directory component yields code 'ENOENT'.
query.title: Error-first callbacks

choices.rationale: `cause` supplied through the options object is defined as a non-enumerable own property, so `Object.keys` never lists it.
`err.cause` is the inner `TypeError` instance, not the outer error, so its `name` is `TypeError`.

console.log(err.cause.name, JSON.stringify(Object.keys(err)));

query.explanation: When an error is constructed with the `{ cause }` options object, V8 installs `cause` as a non-enumerable own property, so it is invisible to `Object.keys`, spread and `JSON.stringify`, even though `err.cause` reads back the value. The cause here is the `TypeError` instance, so `err.cause.name` is `TypeError`.
query.title: Error cause is non-enumerable

query.explanation: An `AssertionError` has `name === 'AssertionError'` (the `[ERR_ASSERTION]` part seen in console output comes from inspection, not from `name`). Its `generatedMessage` flag reports whether assert built the message itself; because an explicit message `'nope'` was passed, the flag is `false`, so the program prints `AssertionError false`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print, and in what order?

choices.rationale: The throw happens on a later timer tick, after the try block has already returned, so the catch clause never runs.
Timer callbacks run only once the synchronous script finishes, so `after` is printed before the exception is raised.
The catch clause is bound to the synchronous `setTimeout` call, not to its callback, so the throw surfaces as an uncaught exception instead.

choices.rationale: Assignment to process.env stores a string, so typeof is never 'number' and `+` concatenates instead of adding.

questions.prompt: Does this program print `"undefined"` with the surrounding double quotes?

questions.rationale: process.env never stores the undefined value itself; it coerces to the string 'undefined', which JSON.stringify prints wrapped in quotes.

choices.rationale: delete removes the key from the environment entirely, so the `in` check reports false afterwards.

questions.rationale: Node sets argv[0] to the absolute executable path, the same string as process.execPath, so the comparison prints true.

choices.rationale: The spread produces an independent plain object, not a live view onto the environment.
The second assignment does update the real environment, so reading process.env.A back gives 2.
process.env's properties are enumerable and own, so spread does copy A into the new object.

process.version is formatted like 'v22.3.0', so it does begin with 'v'.

choices.rationale: chdir changes the process working directory, so the new cwd no longer equals the saved one.
path.basename strips the directory portion and returns only the final segment.
process.cwd() always reports an absolute path, so isAbsolute is true.

choices.rationale: Boolean is applied to the stored string "false", and every non-empty string is truthy, so the third value is true, not false.

Only the printed text looks boolean; the value stored for B is the string "false", and typeof is checked on A, which is also a string.

Reading a variable therefore always yields a string (or undefined if unset), so `typeof process.env.A` is "string". query.explanation: Awaiting a native promise resumes after one microtask tick, but awaiting a plain thenable first queues a resolve-thenable job that calls then(), and only that call schedules the resumption. choices.rationale: Resolving outer's promise with another promise costs extra microtask ticks, so it cannot settle in the first tick.
Returning a promise adds two jobs (resolve-thenable plus its reaction), not one, before outer's promise fulfills.
The surcharge is exactly two ticks, so 'outer' lands between m2 and m3 instead of after the whole chain.

choices.rationale: promisify returns the custom implementation itself rather than a fresh wrapper, so the identity check is true.
The util.promisify.custom symbol takes precedence, so the callback path never supplies the resolved value.
If the callback were wrapped, the resolved value would be 'callback' but the returned wrapper would not equal the custom function.

If present, it returns that function itself (after tagging it), so no callback wrapper is created: the resolved value comes from the custom implementation and the returned function is identical to it.
query.title: util.promisify.custom wins over callback wrapping

choices.rationale: for await awaits the iterator's return() before leaving the loop, so the finally block finishes before 'done' is pushed.
Breaking calls the async iterator's return(), which resumes the generator and does run its finally block.
The break happens right after v === 2, so the generator is closed and never resumes to yield 3.

Promise continuations created inside run() keep the async context, so the microtask also reads A.

query.explanation: The store is bound to the async context created inside run(), so both the promise continuation and the timer callback scheduled there still see it. Code running after run() returns is outside that context and gets undefined, and it executes synchronously before either callback.

choices.rationale: Promise.all does not invoke anything; both tasks already started when the array was built, so the starts are adjacent.
Resumptions run in the order their awaits were queued, and task(2) awaited first, so end2 precedes end1.
Promise.all keeps the input order of the array, so the values join to 21 rather than being sorted ascending.

query.explanation: Both calls run eagerly while the array literal is evaluated, so the synchronous prefixes print back to back. Each await null queues a resumption, and those run in the order they were queued. Promise.all resolves with values in input order, so the result is 21.

query.explanation: events.once attaches a listener for the requested event and also one for 'error' (unless the awaited event is itself 'error'). Emitting 'error' rejects the returned promise with the emitted error, so the await throws and the catch logs its message.
query.title: events.once rejects on an error event

questions.rationale: once() also listens for 'error', so the emit does not become an uncaught exception: the promise rejects with the error and the catch logs 'bad'.

query.explanation: The three timers start concurrently when the array is built, but for await uses the array's synchronous iterator and awaits each element in index order. The loop therefore waits for the 30 ms promise first, and the values are collected in array order, not completion order.
query.title: for await over an array of promises

questions.rationale: for await awaits the elements in index order rather than racing them, so the shorter 10 ms delay does not get its value collected first.

choices.rationale: The abort runs synchronously before the emit, so the promise is already settled as rejected and the later emit cannot resolve it.
Aborting does not just reject: events.once also detaches the internal 'data' and 'error' listeners it installed, leaving the count at 0.
The rejection value is a DOMException-style AbortError whose code is ABORT_ERR, not a plain Error with code ERR_ABORTED.

query.explanation: events.once(emitter, name, { signal }) wires an abort listener onto the signal. Calling ac.abort() runs that listener synchronously, which removes the temporary 'data' and 'error' listeners and rejects the promise with an AbortError (name 'AbortError', code 'ABORT_ERR'). Because the promise is already rejected, the subsequent ee.emit('data', 1) has no listener to notify and cannot change the outcome, so the catch block runs and listenerCount('data') is 0.
query.title: Aborting an events.once promise
